papers.title: Embedding kernels for sequence-function relationships
papers.abstract: A central challenge in biology is understanding how variation in biological sequences (DNA, RNA, and protein) impacts function. Recent advances in high-throughput techniques have enabled the measurement of such sequence-function relationships on an unprecedented scale. However, analyzing these complex datasets requires models that are both flexible and mathematically tractable. We consider Gaussian process regression, a Bayesian method that specifies a Gaussian prior distribution over sequence-function relationships. The prior is defined by a kernel function that encodes the expected covariance between pairs of sequences. We study a family of embedding kernels in which the covariance depends on the distance between sequences in a learned embedding space, making these kernels both expressive and interpretable. We show that linear embedding kernels generalize previously studied classes of kernels and can more flexibly express variability in the expected similarity between mutational effects across genetic backgrounds, allowing the resulting priors to encode more complex biological mechanisms such as RNA base-pairing. We implement these methods using a GPU-accelerated Gaussian process framework, allowing us to learn linear embeddings and make predictions with datasets containing hundreds of thousands of measurements. We find that our embedding kernels match or improve the predictive performance of other kernels across various high-throughput sequence-function datasets, including protein datasets ranging from short motifs to full-length proteins. Furthermore, the learned embedding spaces provide insight into biological mechanisms underlying sequence-function relationships.

papers.title: Global Epistasis Constrains the Dynamics of Fitness in Multiple Environments
papers.abstract: Adaptive mutations in one (home) environment often have diverse effects in other (non-home) environments. This so-called pleiotropy has important implications for the ability of populations to survive environmental fluctuations, which are common in nature. But how the fitness effects vary across mutations, genetic backgrounds and environments is poorly characterized empirically, and a unifying theory describing this variation is lacking. To address this gap, we develop the so-called global epistasis family of models and find that it explains a substantial proportion of variation in the distributions of mutational effects across genetic backgrounds and environments in a published yeast dataset. We then examine evolutionary dynamics that emerge in this model and we find that, as a population adapts at home, its non-home fitness can either converge to an intermediate finite value, or increase or decline indefinitely, with the empirical parameters being consistent with the first two outcomes. This work provides a quantitative unification of pleiotropy and epistasis, generates testable predictions for the pleiotropic consequences of adaptation and enables a better understanding of evolution in fluctuating environments.

papers.title: SOX4 suppresses vascular calcification via DNA-binding-independent regulation of the USP10-HNRNPC-WNT5A axis
papers.abstract: Background: Vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) osteogenic differentiation drives vascular calcification, yet the endogenous mechanisms that restrain this transition remain poorly defined. SOX4 has recently emerged as a regulator of phenotype switching in endothelial and epithelial cells, but whether it governs VSMC fate and vascular calcification is unknown. Methods: SOX4 expression was examined in human calcified arteries, in vitamin D3 (VitD3)-treated mouse aortas and in phosphate-treated human aortic smooth muscle cells. Loss- and gain-of-function experiments, an HMG-box-deleted SOX4 mutant, co-immunoprecipitation combined with mass spectrometry, ubiquitination and protein stability assays, RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing and mRNA decay assays were combined with VSMC-specific Sox4 knockout mice and pharmacological WNT5A inhibition. Results: SOX4 protein was upregulated in calcified VSMCs and arteries, yet SOX4 loss aggravated and SOX4 overexpression attenuated VSMC osteogenic differentiation. A SOX4 mutant lacking the HMG-box retained anti-calcific activity, placing the function outside DNA binding. SOX4 interacted with HNRNPC and attenuated the HNRNPC-USP10 association, promoting K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of HNRNPC. HNRNPC bound WNT5A mRNA and was required for its stability, so that SOX4 reduced WNT5A expression. VSMC-specific Sox4 deletion aggravated VitD3-induced aortic calcification together with HNRNPC and WNT5A upregulation. Strengthening this braking axis with the WNT5A antagonist BOX5 attenuated VSMC osteogenic differentiation in vitro and vascular calcification in vivo in both genotypes, identifying WNT5A as a pharmacologically accessible node downstream of SOX4 loss. Conclusions: SOX4 restrains VSMC osteogenic differentiation through post-transcriptional control of cell fate, defining a SOX4-HNRNPC-WNT5A axis and identifying it as a pharmacologically accessible target for vascular calcification.

papers.title: An iron acquisition system promotes Bifidobacterium longum fitness in competitive early life gut communities
papers.abstract: Iron availability influences the composition of the gut microbiota, yet the mechanisms that enable beneficial bacteria to acquire iron and compete within iron-variable communities remain poorly understood. Here, we identify Fei (Fe import), an iron-responsive acquisition system that promotes the fitness of Bifidobacterium longum subsp. longum, a prevalent member of the early-life gut microbiota. Comparative profiling of 20 bifidobacterial strains revealed substantial inter- and intraspecies variation in growth under iron limitation, with multiple B. longum subsp. longum strains maintaining comparatively robust growth. Transcriptomic analysis identified a four-gene locus, feiMQOX, that was strongly induced during iron depletion and returned towards control expression following iron supplementation. The complete locus was highly conserved within B. longum subsp. longum but unevenly distributed across the wider genus. Disruption of individual Fei components impaired growth and reduced cell-associated iron under iron-restricted conditions, while metal-binding studies of purified FeiX demonstrated a physiological preference for Fe(II). FeiX also provided a pronounced fitness advantage during competition with an infant-derived Enterococcus faecalis isolate, particularly under iron limitation. Finally, analysis of longitudinal metagenomic data from Bangladeshi infants demonstrated that Fei is present within infant gut communities and that its abundance changes following iron supplementation. Together, these findings identify a lineage-associated iron-acquisition system that connects micronutrient availability with bifidobacterial physiology and competitive fitness. More broadly, our findings establish strain-level micronutrient acquisition as a potentially important determinant of beneficial bacterial fitness within the developing gut microbiota.

papers.title: Emergence of a Novel Bacteriophage of Toxigenic Vibrio cholerae in Haiti
papers.abstract: Toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae O1 are facultative pathogens that persist in estuaries and cause the secretory diarrheal disease cholera. Virulent bacteriophages (phages) can modulate pathogen density in both humans and aquatic reservoirs, thereby reducing cholera transmission. We report a novel phage, MAA01, isolated from cholera stool and environmental water samples collected in Haiti. The MAA01 genome is double-stranded DNA (31,507 base pairs) and contains 47 genes. Based on transmission electron microscopy morphology and phylogenetic analysis, we classify the novel phage as a member of the Caudoviricetes class. Its genome content is consistent with a temperate lifestyle, yet we observed a virulent phenotype in all strains tested, including toxigenic and non-toxigenic environmental O1 serogroup strains. Sequence analysis of spontaneous escape mutants of V. cholerae identified the O1 lipopolysaccharide antigen as the phage receptor. Using an infant mouse model of intestinal colonization, we showed that MAA01 can reduce V. cholerae load by 4-fold, indicating it can prey on its host in the small intestine.

papers.title: Energetic niches of syntrophic methanogens recorded by clumped isotopes
papers.abstract: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, an important energy source and a potential biosignature in extraterrestrial environments. Stable carbon and hydrogen isotope ({delta}13C and {delta}D) and clumped isotopologues ({triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2) compositions of methane have been widely used as tracers for methanogenesis pathways. Furthermore, isotopic signatures of methane typically shift closer to equilibrium as the Gibbs energy ({triangleup}Gr) of methanogenesis moves closer to the energy limit of life. However, the variations of clumped methane isotope signatures in response to the changes in {triangleup}Gr lack careful examination. In this study, we measure the isotope signatures of methane produced by monoculture methanogens with formate or H2/CO2, and by syntrophic cocultures of hydrogenotrophic methanogens paired with acetate or propionate oxidizers. Methanogenesis by cocultures has lower Gibbs energy yield than monocultures, yet both {triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2 values from cocultures are further away from isotopic equilibrium. From these experiments, we identify an energetic niche ({triangleup}Gr ~ -35 kJ mol-1 CH4), where {delta}13C, {triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2 values of hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis transiently exhibit more disequilibrium. This study presents differential responses of bulk carbon, hydrogen and clumped isotopic signatures to {triangleup}Gr, and highlights their applications in distinguishing methanogenesis under different energy regimes.

papers.title: Identification and characterization of a Streptococcus strain isolated from the esophagus of an adult male heterozygous for the CF allele
papers.abstract: The genus Streptococcus consists of diverse bacteria that are integral components of the human microbiome, acting as both important commensals and opportunistic pathogens. In this study, one strain of an -hemolytic species of the genus Streptococcus, GP0011T, isolated from an esophageal aspirate collected during an endoscopy, was characterised phenotypically to establish its taxonomic status. The strain was isolated from an adult male heterozygous for a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) mutation. The phylogenetic analysis indicates that the strain is a novel species within the mitis group, with Streptococcus oralis ATCC 35037T being the closest relative with 94.84% average nucleotide identity (ANI) and 58.3% digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH). Phenotypic characterization and API20 Strep strips distinguished GP0011T from S. oralis by the absence of alkaline phosphatase activity, trehalose fermentation, and starch fermentation, and by superior growth on D-mannitol and D-sorbitol, consistent with genomic data. The strain is Gram-positive, catalase-negative, and the cells are ovoid with a mean cell diameter of 1.3 {micro}m. Growth occurred at 25-43 C, with an optimum at 30 C, with an optimum at pH 8.0. Antibiotic resistance genes msrD and mefA, conferring resistance to azithromycin and erythromycin, as well as pathways for mannitol and sorbitol metabolism, were found and phenotypically confirmed in the GP0011T genome but were absent from S. oralis. These findings indicate that GP0011T represents a novel species within the genus Streptococcus with the proposed name of Streptococcus ruoffae sp. nov. The type strain is GP0011T (ATCC TSD-627 and NCTC 15312).

papers.title: Genomic blueprints of a dynamic deep sea: contrasting adaptive strategies potentially drive seasonal microbial succession
papers.abstract: Genetic variation within marine microbial populations can help reveal how deep-sea communities respond to environmental change. However, population-level genomic variation in deep pelagic waters remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic datasets from ~1,080 m depth in the South China Sea to compare genomic variation between summer and winter microbial assemblages. Among 11 persistent metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) detected in both summer and winter samples, we observed differences in abundance, nucleotide diversity ({pi}), pN/pS ratios, and gene-level differentiation. Two enriched populations showed contrasting patterns, with Sphingobium yanoikuyae enriched in winter samples and Methyloversatilis universalis enriched in summer samples. The winter-enriched S. yanoikuyae population carried winter-associated accessory genes related to restriction-modification and toxin-antitoxin systems, consistent with a defense-oriented persistence profile. In contrast, the summer-enriched M. universalis population showed higher nucleotide diversity in summer samples and divergence in genes related to motility, transport, and cobalamin acquisition. Across persistent MAGs, low pN/pS ratios indicated predominantly purifying selection, whereas gene-specific divergence and flexible accessory gene content suggested population-level adaptive potential under contrasting winter and summer conditions. These results reveal population-genomic differences associated with winter-summer microbial shifts in the deep sea.

papers.title: Integrating multi-omics data and machine learning in single-step GBLUP reaction norm models to improve prediction across untested environments in lodgepole pine
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of genomic prediction in forest trees is often constrained by genotype-by-environment (GE) interactions, particularly when predicting performance in environments not represented in the training population. We evaluated the integration of genomic, enviromic (climatic and soil), and metabolomic (targeted monoterpene) information within multi-environment single-step genomic best linear unbiased prediction (ssGBLUP) reaction norm models to improve prediction in unobserved environments. Models incorporated environmental covariates (W) and genotype-specific responses using linear and nonlinear kernels, including Gaussian and Arc-Cosine formulations. The study examined 12 traits measured on 11,124 trees across four lodgepole pine progeny trials, with 1,490 trees genotyped with 25,099 SNPs. Predictive performance was assessed using leave-one-environment-out cross-validation. Additive genetic correlations among environments revealed substantial GE for early-growth traits and drought-related decline, with correlations frequently below 0.65. Inclusion of environmental covariates reduced variance attributed to site effects, indicating that these descriptors captured environmental heterogeneity. Incorporating GE and genotype-by-environmental covariate (GW) interactions improved model performance, increasing explained phenotypic variance by up to 29.58% and reducing residual variance by up to 3.13% relative to baseline models. Across traits, GE explained more phenotypic variation than GW, contributing on average 2.31% and 0.60%, respectively. Predictive ability was high across models (0.688-0.701), with gains of up to 7.85% when nonlinear kernels were combined with metabolomic covariates, particularly for traits exhibiting stronger GE. Monoterpene profiles yielded predictive performance comparable to climate and soil descriptors, highlighting the potential of integrating genomic, enviromic, and metabolomic information to improve prediction across environments and support climate-resilient forest tree breeding and deployment.

papers.title: Magnetic separation screens identify G alpha 15 as a central regulator of degranulation downstream of neutrophil chemoattractant receptors
papers.abstract: Neutrophil recruitment and effector functions protect the body from infection. However, their excessive activity is central to inflammatory diseases, in which neutrophil granule proteins damage tissues and amplify inflammation. These proteins are released through degranulation, a regulated secretion process that can be triggered by the same chemoattractant molecules that drive neutrophil recruitment. Neutrophils detect attractants using G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that signal through Gi G-proteins. How the activity of these receptors is channeled to promote degranulation versus chemotaxis in the proper contexts remains unclear. Here, we identify positive and negative regulators of degranulation in HL-60 neutrophils using genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens that exploit the transient surface exposure of granule membrane proteins. We identify G15 as a critical degranulation-specific effector of the attractant GPCRs FPR1 and LTB4R, and branched actin assembly as the dominant process limiting degranulation. Our results suggest that use of a second G subunit allows a switch to the degranulation output.

papers.title: A histone hitchhiking mechanism for chromatin maintenance during mammalian transcription elongation
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic transcription machinery faces the dual challenge of having to dismantle the nucleosome barrier for efficient elongation and faithfully restore the chromatin landscape in its wake to prevent aberrant transcription. The sequence of molecular events from nucleosome unwrapping to reassembly has yet to be delineated. Here, we use a single-molecule platform to visualize the dynamics of chromatin transcription by mammalian elongation complex (EC) in real time. When supplemented with a set of elongation factors and histone chaperones, the EC can efficiently traverse the nucleosome it encounters and, surprisingly, carry the dislodged histones while continuing translocation on DNA, a phenomenon we termed histone 'hitchhiking'. The formation of this hitchhiking complex is facilitated by the elongation factor SPT6 and IWS1 through distinct mechanisms. On the other hand, the histone chaperones FACT and NAP1L1 promote the transition from histone hitchhiking to nucleosome reassembly. We further showed that the next nucleosome presents a strong barrier against the hitchhiking complex, thus limiting long-range chromatin disruption. Overall, our results revealed that histone hitchhiking by EC is a prevalent intermediate during chromatin transcription, and the timing and location of its resolution are tuned by multiple factors. This mechanism may provide the robustness and flexibility needed to maintain the local organization of transcriptionally active chromatin.

papers.title: Alkyladenine DNA glycosylase regulates TDG-mediated demethylation and neuronal gene expression by competitive substrate binding
papers.abstract: Endogenous single-strand DNA breaks (SSBs) that arise during active DNA demethylation, regulate neurodevelopmental gene expression. Thymine (TDG) and alkyladenine (AAG) DNA glycosylases recognize oxidized methylcytosines. While TDG is required for excision, role of AAG in active demethylation and neurodevelopment remains unknown. Using mouse neurospheres, hippocampus, and human induced neurons (iNs), we show that AAG is needed for neurogenesis. Loss of AAG contributes to delayed neurodevelopmental and premature synaptic gene expression, evident from single-cell RNA sequencing of differentiating iNs. Synaptic gene expression is co-regulated by both AAG and TDG, with loss of single glycosylase inducing an opposing effect, implying competition. Single-molecule and biochemical assays directly demonstrate this competition, with AAG inhibiting TDG on 5fC. Without AAG, TDG has higher affinity, resulting in reduced global 5fC and increased SSB intermediates. In summary, AAG substrate competition plays an important role in fine tuning active demethylation, thereby regulating gene expression and DNA breaks during neurogenesis.

papers.title: Formate, hydrogen, and acetate shape the morphology, physiology and lifestyles of the host-associated methanogen Methanobrevibacter smithii
papers.abstract: Methane-producing archaea (methanogens) are increasingly linked to gastrointestinal, neuropsychiatric, and neurodevelopmental disorders. These conditions are often associated with altered microbial metabolism that changes the availability of acetate, formate, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane in the gut. However, the physiological importance of formate and acetate in host-associated methanogens remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to interpret microbiome data and infer functions and cross-domain interactions of methanogens in health and disease. Here, we investigated the physiological and metabolic capabilities of Methanobrevibacter smithii, the predominant methanogen of the human gut. Formate limitation altered growth, morphology, extracellular pH, gas metabolism, and cellular organization, and induced the formation of cell aggregates. Although acetate was consumed only in small quantities (nmol), its availability significantly influenced growth, gas metabolism, extracellular pH, and formate utilization, indicating functions that extend beyond its role as a biosynthetic precursor. Conversely, nutrient excess promoted a transition to a biofilm lifestyle, suggesting that biofilm formation may function as a carbon sink. We further developed Msm_MEP, an experimentally refined genome-scale metabolic model based on the AGORA2 reconstruction, which captures the metabolic capabilities of M. smithii, quantifies ATP allocation across cellular processes, and predicts the phenotypic consequences of gene deletions. Together, our findings identify formate, hydrogen, and acetate as interacting determinants of M. smithii physiology and suggest metabolite-dependent transitions between planktonic growth, cell aggregation, and biofilm formation. Our results establish a framework for interpreting microbiome data and understanding how environmental metabolites shape archaea physiology and cross-domain interactions within the human microbiome.

papers.title: TRIM5α, TRIM56 and TRIM69 differentially regulate dengue virus 2 infection through selective NS2B3-mediated antagonism
papers.abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is a major mosquito-borne human pathogen. Understanding the mechanisms of cellular resistance to the infection is vital to develop novel therapeutic tools. Tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins contribute to antiviral innate immunity through direct restriction of viral replication and regulation of antiviral signaling, but current knowledge on DENV targeting by TRIM proteins remains preliminary. Previously, TRIM56 was found to inhibit DENV, whereas reports on whether TRIM69 is a DENV restriction factor are conflicting. Surprisingly, the broad-spectrum viral restriction factor TRIM5 was proposed to restrict tick-borne but not mosquito-borne flaviviruses. Here, we investigated the effects of TRIM5, TRIM56, and TRIM69 on DENV serotype 2 (DENV2) infection. Overexpression experiments showed that TRIM5 and TRIM56 restrict DENV2, whereas TRIM69 enhances it. Consistently, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function showed that knocking out TRIM5 or TRIM56 increases infection, while TRIM69 knockout decreases it. Restriction correlated with reduced viral RNA and viral protein levels in TRIM5- and TRIM56-expressing cells. Virus-free experiments showed that TRIM56 downregulates the DENV2 protease complex NS2B3 levels. Reciprocally, DENV2 NS2B3 reduced TRIM56 and TRIM69 abundance independently of protease activity. RING domain-mutated TRIM56 retained partial antiviral activity and the ability to reduce NS2B3 levels, and TRIM56-NS2B3 reciprocal downmodulation effects were not counteracted by proteasomal or lysosomal inhibition. Together, these findings establish TRIM5 as a DENV2 restriction factor, reveal TRIM69 as a positive factor in DENV2 infection, suggest that TRIM5? and TRIM56 inhibit DENV2 through distinct mechanisms, and hint at proteasome-independent TRIM56-NS2B3 reciprocal downmodulation.

papers.title: Precision in Predicting Catalytic Performance of Medium Chain Dehydrogenase: A Benchmark Data Set and Comparative Metrics
papers.abstract: Medium-chain dehydrogenases/reductases are highly versatile oxidoreductases with broad industrial relevance but complex structure-function relationships that continue to challenge catalytic performance prediction. A Benchmark for Medium-Chain Dehydrogenases (MCDBench) is introduced as a rigorously curated benchmark dataset comprising 792 enzyme-substrate-cofactor combinations, including experimentally validated inactive cases obtained under standardized conditions. MCDBench spans 36 chemically diverse alcohol substrates, representative MDR subclasses, and multiple cofactor types, enabling systematic evaluation of model generalization. Benchmarking four representative activity-prediction models (DLKcat, UniKP, TurNuP, and CataPro) shows that correlations with experimental activities remain modest under standardized conditions, and that distinguishing active from inactive catalytic space remains a practical challenge across enzyme classes and substrate types. Analysis points to a positive-data skew inherited from widely used biochemical databases and the relative scarcity of validated negative samples as key factors shaping this behavior. By providing a standardized benchmark that integrates experimentally validated negative cases, MCDBench offers a unified experimental and computational framework to help the field measure and further improve the discrimination of active and inactive catalytic space for biocatalyst design.

papers.title: Adaptive signal evolution and gene flow drive variable speciation outcomes in bark anoles
papers.abstract: New species evolve in a complex and non-linear fashion, resulting in situations where genomic and phenotypic variation between diverging lineages become decoupled. For example, natural selection acting on traits commonly used to diagnose species can instead drive trait variation to disagree with genomic evidence for species boundaries, challenging systematists aiming to delimit species. In this study, we combine phylogenetic, population genomic, and coalescent-based gene flow analyses to test whether convergence of a signaling trait has a shared genomic basis and to evaluate the evidence for unrecognized species level diversity in the Anolis distichus species group, a polytypic clade of lizards spanning the island of Hispaniola and the Bahamas in which diversity of a sex-linked signaling trait conflicts with genetic evidence for species boundaries. Comparing evolutionary histories of autosomes, sex chromosomes, and mitochondrial DNA, we find that the entire spectrum of signaling trait variation is present in four major geographic clades of the A. distichus species group and recover support for the independent evolution of this convergent signal. By quantifying isolation-by-distance and inferring migration across all contact zones on Hispaniola, we find evidence for lineages spanning the entire speciation continuum---from interbreeding populations to lineages exhibiting signatures of strong reproductive isolation. Together, our study highlights how phenotypic and genomic divergence may decouple during speciation, and provides a robust framework for gene flow-informed taxonomic revisions of the A. distichus species group.

papers.title: Nuclear blebs are rupture-prone restricted compartments of the nucleus
papers.abstract: Nuclear blebs are abnormal herniations of the cell nucleus that cause nuclear rupture and dysfunction. The biophysical principles underlying nuclear blebs and ruptures remain to be fully elucidated. Using nuclear localization signal green fluorescent protein (NLS-GFP) we tracked nuclear bleb rupture dynamics. Upon nuclear rupture, the nuclear bleb NLS-GFP loss rate is significantly faster than the nuclear body, whereas non-blebbed nuclei ruptures show no difference in NLS-GFP loss rates between the site of nuclear rupture and body. Micromanipulation compression induced nuclear bleb rupture recapitulates 5-fold nuclear bleb loss rate. Furthermore, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) in the intact nuclear bleb is significantly slower than recovery in the nuclear body. Confocal imaging reveals that the transition from the nuclear bleb to body is significantly constrained. Thus, we reveal the nuclear bleb as a restricted compartment and nuclear rupture site, both of which greatly affect nuclear functions.

papers.title: Intestinal epithelial differentiation factor HNF4α restrains homeostatic interferon signaling and is required for its full induction during Salmonella infection
papers.abstract: Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) must interpret microbial signals to transcriptionally adapt their identity and function. Which transcription factors (TFs) mediate those adaptations, and whether competing transcriptional pathways signal within the same or in different IEC subpopulations, remains unclear. We find that microbiota colonization shifts nearly all IECs toward an interferon-driven inflammatory program at the expense of genes involved in enterocyte differentiation and metabolism. These opposing gene expression programs are associated with different TF motifs and are inversely correlated within individual cells. We discover that HNF4, a TF central to enterocyte differentiation, acts as a brake on interferon signaling in vitro. In accord, loss of HNF4 in IECs in mice elevates baseline interferon-stimulated gene expression but prevents its full induction during infection with the bacterial pathogen Salmonella. Together our findings reveal a novel mechanism by which opposing intestinal epithelial differentiation and interferon signaling programs interact within the same cell to maintain proper transcriptional control and homeostasis.

papers.title: Capsular surveillance-guided phage cocktails against carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
papers.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is among the most urgent antimicrobial-resistance threats, yet its extraordinary capsular diversity has kept phage therapy locked in per-isolate matching-a process too slow and labor-intensive for routine use. Here we convert this specificity problem into a look-up problem. Interrogating 26,138 CRKP genomes from 96 countries, we show that capsular diversity collapses onto a tractable target list: 14 capsular locus (KL) types dominate contemporary circulation and jointly account for 67-77% of the CRKP burden in every WHO region, stably from 2010 to 2024 and after removal of sampling bias. We assembled a repository of 48 strictly lytic phages spanning all 14 types and organized it into capsule-defined modules: for eight KL types a single capsule-targeting phage sufficed to prevent resistant regrowth over 24 h, and for the remaining six a two-phage module pairs a capsule-targeting phage with a capsule-independent phage that recognizes the second receptor layer exposed upon capsule loss. We treated 28 clinical isolates, covering two distinct STs for each of the 14 KL types. Modules were assigned from the KL call alone, without isolate-level matching data. Growth was suppressed in every strain, and ST background had no significant effect in 12 of 14 types. These results establish capsule type, not lineage, as the operative unit of CRKP phage preparedness: a single rapid KL-typing step converts a diagnostic result into a therapeutic decision, providing a practical, lineage-agnostic route from surveillance to treatment.

papers.title: Treponema pallidum eight-stranded beta-barrels: an evolving, versatile family of outer membrane proteins in the service of stealth pathogenicity.
papers.abstract: Syphilis is a multistage sexually transmitted infection caused by the highly invasive and immunoevasive spirochete Treponema pallidum (TPA). TPA depends on the import of many host-derived nutrients to sustain its auxotrophic lifestyle. Moreover, its invasive nature requires interactions with diverse host molecules to successfully disseminate and persist. The outer membrane proteins (OMPs) mediating these processes remain largely uncharacterized. In other bacteria, 8-stranded {beta}-barrels (8S{beta}Bs) perform such functions, including nutrient uptake and host interactions. Here, we investigated the composition, structural diversity and evolutionary dynamics of the 8S{beta}B family in TPA. Reexamination of the TPA OMPeome revealed four previously unrecognized members in addition to the four known 8SBs, expanding the family to eight members. Based on RNAseq, all eight were transcribed in treponemes harvested from rabbit testes. Predicted structures revealed substantial differences in channel properties and extracellular loop (ECL) architecture, consistent with functional diversification. AlphaFold 3 modeling predicted interactions with diverse host molecules implicated in nutrient uptake, adherence, and immune regulation, providing testable hypotheses for the functional specialization of individual 8SBBBs. Despite containing predicted B-cell epitopes, most TPA 8S{beta}B ECLs exhibited limited antigenicity during rabbit infection. Analysis of global clinical strains revealed distinct patterns of sequence variation across the 8S{beta}B family, although most were highly conserved and appeared to be under purifying selection. Variation within hypermutable intragenic polyguanosine tracts emerged as an additional potential mechanism for modulating 8S{beta}B repertoire composition. Our findings highlight the 8S{beta}B family as an important component of the molecular architecture underlying TPA stealth pathogenicity and reveal an ongoing mechanism through which the spirochete diversifies its OMP repertoire within circulating populations.

papers.title: Programmed ribosomal frameshifting regulates tissue-specific pioneer activity
papers.abstract: Pioneer transcription factors bind nucleosomal DNA and establish accessible chromatin, yet their binding is tissue specific. While studies have largely focused on protein-extrinsic features, like chromatin structure and cofactor expression, the mechanisms governing the tissue-specific binding remain poorly understood. We used the Drosophila pioneer transcription factor Zelda as a paradigm to investigate the mechanisms controlling tissue-specific binding. Zelda promotes the undifferentiated state in both the embryo and in neural stem cells of the larval brain. However, Zelda binds thousands of unique sites in each tissue and, in so doing, defines tissue-specific enhancers. We showed that tissue-specific binding is controlled by the developmentally regulated use of two distinct DNA-binding domains. Our identification of a novel, neural stem cell enriched Zelda proteoform that lacks the embryo-specific C-terminal DNA-binding domain explains the differential DNA-binding domain usage. This proteoform arises through developmentally regulated -1 ribosomal frameshifting, a mechanism common to viruses but not documented for any eukaryotic transcription factors. Together we revealed a new strategy where developmentally programmed ribosomal frameshifting confers tissue-specific pioneer-factor binding and suggest that this mechanism may be more broadly used to diversify the proteome than previously appreciated.

papers.title: Progerin Expression in Alveolar Epithelial Cells Exacerbates Inflammatory Responses to SARS-CoV-2 Infection
papers.abstract: Age is a major determinant of severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), yet the cell-intrinsic consequences of ageing for SARS-CoV-2 infection remain difficult to examine in human experimental systems. Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived tissues provide accessible models of infection but generally lack hallmarks of ageing. Here, we employed an iPSC line containing an inducible progerin cassette and differentiated these cells towards an alveolar type II-like epithelial fate. Progerin induction in differentiated cells increased DNA-damage-associated {gamma}H2AX staining and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, reduced the heterochromatin-associated mark H3K9me3, and induced transcriptional programs associated with extracellular matrix remodeling, fibrosis and inflammation. Following infection with authentic SARS-CoV-2, progerin-expressing cultures exhibited a greater perturbation of the host transcriptome, including increased interferon-associated and inflammatory gene signatures. Transcriptomic analysis support higher viral RNA abundance in the aged model, and this was further confirmed by functional assays that showed increased infectious activity from condition media. Together, these data establish a temporally controlled model of selected ageing-associated phenotypes in human alveolar epithelial-like cells and suggest that progerin-induced cellular stress can amplify epithelial responses to SARS-CoV-2. More broadly, these findings distinguish epithelial-intrinsic inflammatory priming from the multicellular pathology of severe COVID-19.

papers.title: Differential modulation of host cell Serine and Arginine-Rich (SR) protein and apoptotic factor BCL-2 gene expressions during Chandipura and Dengue virus infections
papers.abstract: Regulation of alternative splicing (AS) is important in controlling cellular functions. More than 95% human genes are alternatively spliced and AS is regulated by close to 100 splicing factors. Line of evidences suggest that virus infections alter the AS pattern of numerous host genes. In this study we have investigated Chandipura virus (CHPV) induced alteration of host cell SR protein gene expressions and determined if these changes have any effect on apoptotic factor BCL-2 levels. CHPV is a negative stranded RNA virus which causes fever, brain encephalitis and death among young children with a case-fatality rate of 50%. Few studies were done in past to understand the roles of host factors in CHPV pathogenesis and no study was done on virus induced changes in AS. Our study showed that there is a down-regulation of SR proteins SRp55 and SRp75 expression levels significantly decreased in the CHPV infected Vero E6 cells compared to uninfected cells. For a comparison, we also looked at the levels of SRp55 and SRp75 in dengue virus (DENV) infected cells. Our results showed that SRp75 levels is unchanged whereas SRp55 levels increased in DENV infected cells. We have also determined the levels of large and small splice variants of apoptotic gene BCL-2 to find out possible correlation between the altered splicing factor expressions and virus infected cell death via apoptosis. Our data indicates that in CHPV infected cells, BCL-2 large splice variant expressions decreased as compared to uninfected cells. This is the first study of CHPV mediated alteration of splicing factor expressions and these results warrant further study with other viruses to better understand the global changes in host splicing events, cell survival, host immune response during virus infection.

papers.title: Development of an Enclosed Microbial Co-culture Device and GCXGC-TOFMS Workflow to Investigate Volatile Organic Compound Exchange
papers.abstract: Microbial volatile organic compounds (mVOCs) can mediate interactions between microorganisms without direct physical contact. However, co-culture systems to examine these interactions are limited, and volatilomic data interpretation is challenging. Here, we developed enclosed microbial co-culture platforms compatible with diverse microbial systems, headspace solid-phase microextraction (HS-SPME), and comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GCXGC-TOFMS) for mVOC sampling and characterization. In a double-layer co-culture device, diffusion of exogenously supplemented Aspergillus fumigatus mVOCs, 1-octen-3-ol and isopentyl alcohol, inhibited Pseudomonas aeruginosa growth and biofilm formation. The device was then used to examine mVOC-mediated interkingdom interactions between the bacterium P. aeruginosa and the spore-forming fungus A. fumigatus. GCXGC-TOFMS was used to profile mVOCs in four sample classes: media, each individual monoculture, and co-culture. Tile-based F-ratio analysis identified 198 analyte hits that differed across at least two of the four sample classes. Subsequent ANOVA identified 104 of these analytes as statistically significant (p < 0.01). To systematically classify their abundance patterns, pairwise comparisons among the four sample classes were encoded using a six-digit ternary code representing the direction and statistical significance of each difference. Of the 104 significant analytes, 88 were assigned to 15 recurring ternary-code groups, capturing distinct patterns associated with microbial production, suppression in co-culture, and differential consumption of media-derived compounds. Closely related ternary-code groups were further consolidated into five major Categories, providing biologically interpretable mVOC profiles. Overall, the integrated co-culture platform and analytical approach provide a versatile framework for investigating microbial volatile interactions and interpreting complex multidimensional volatilomic datasets.

papers.title: An Optimized ChIP-sequencing protocol for transcription factors in embryonic mouse brains
papers.abstract: Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-Seq) is widely used to identify genome-wide protein-chromatin interactions. However, obtaining reliable ChIP-seq data for transcription factors has been challenging for several reasons, including their low abundance, transient or weak DNA binding, and poor antibody performance. Here, we present an improved ChIP-Seq protocol for mapping transcription factor occupancy in embryonic mouse brains. We describe critical steps in tissue preparation, fixation and antigen unmasking steps, and chromatin fragmentation by prolonged sonication, specifically optimized for transcription factors. Our key innovation is the application of antigen retrieval to freshly fixed tissues, a technique commonly used in immunohistochemistry to unmask epitopes masked by fixation, in combination with slow fixation and extensive sonication to enhance ChIP-seq performance. This approach enhances epitope accessibility and expands the range of antibodies suitable for ChIP-seq, providing a robust strategy for mapping the genome-wide occupancy of transcription factors that are otherwise challenging to study using conventional ChIP-seq methods.

papers.title: Periodic spatial patterning of gene expression via a natural quorum-synchronized oscillator
papers.abstract: In many biological systems, genetic oscillators that function in growing tissues can establish spatially repetitive patterns of gene expression. However, few mechanisms for generating such patterns are known in bacteria. Here, we describe an oscillator within the quorum sensing circuit of Streptomyces coelicolor. Through modeling and genetic experiments, we demonstrate that this quorum oscillator controls periodic expression of a gene involved in antibiotic biosynthesis at the periphery of expanding colonies. We show that environmental factors, namely small molecule diffusabilty and carrying capacity, independently modulate the oscillator frequency and amplitude, respectively. The architecture of the quorum oscillator imbues this "clock" with three emergent features; it is synchronized locally across cells, only advances due to collective cellular communication, and its dynamics are directly responsive to environmental conditions.

papers.title: Metabolic rewiring of sugar alcohols drives lichen symbiosis in Trebouxiophyceae microalgae
papers.abstract: Lichen symbioses are among the most successful mutualisms in extreme environments, yet the biochemical traits that enable algal partners to thrive within them remain poorly defined. We used untargeted GC-MS to uncover metabolic rules underlying symbiotic compatibility. Comparing 21 Trebouxiophyceae species, including free-living microalgae and lichen photobionts, we identified 260 metabolites, concluding that sugar alcohol metabolism emerged as the principal axis of differentiation, with ribitol-rich taxa consistently dominating lichen partnerships. High ribitol producers shared a coordinated metabolic program coupling elevated malate with compatible solutes (glycerol, inositol, proline) and phospholipid intermediates, supporting osmoprotection, redox balance, and membrane remodeling. They released ribitol into the culture medium together with a distinctive suite of metabolites (including maltose, allulose, and tyramine) not previously reported in lichen algae, suggesting new candidates for symbiotic signaling. A comparative analysis of Ramalina farinacea and its photobiont, Trebouxia jamesii, revealed a metabolic shift in symbiosis towards sustained arabitol, ribitol, and sucrose accumulation, and away from glucose accumulation, indicating an adaptive carbon-allocation strategy. These findings identify ribitol-centered metabolic rewiring as a pivotal trait for lichenization, provide mechanistic insight into stress resilience and partner specificity, and establish metabolomic profiling as a predictive framework for chemotaxonomy and testing algal-fungal compatibility in symbiotic systems.

papers.title: Optimal combined chemotherapeutic and antibiotic treatment for cancer in the presence of saboteur bacteria
papers.abstract: We consider a mathematical model of cancer dynamics under chemotherapeutic treatment in the presence of bacteria capable of metabolizing the chemotherapeutic agent, thereby compromising therapeutic efficacy. To counteract this effect, we investigate the introduction of antibiotic co-therapy aimed at eradicating the bacterial population or at least mitigating its negative impact on treatment outcomes. The underlying dynamics are formulated as a system of four non-linear ordinary differential equations, with the time-varying dosages of both drugs treated as control variables. Applying optimal control theory, we explore which combined treatment strategy leads to the best outcome, and how it is influenced by the model parameters. Convergence to the optimal control is achieved by employing a relaxation method within the forward-backward sweep algorithm. Furthermore, we analyze a discrete-dose variant of the optimal control problem, providing a more clinically realistic framework for scheduled drug administration.

papers.title: LIFE-seq: longitudinal spatial transcriptomics of living tissue
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has deepened our understanding of cellular spatial heterogeneity, yet existing technologies are predominantly confined to fixed or frozen specimens, limiting longitudinal molecular profiling of the same living tissue. To overcome this limitation, we developed LIFE-seq (Living-tissue in situ nanoforest extraction for spatiotemporal transcriptomic mapping), a minimally invasive approach that combines high-density nanoforest arrays for molecular sampling with directed transfer onto spatially barcoded messenger RNA (mRNA) capture chips. LIFE-seq enables spatial transcriptomic profiling while preserving overall tissue integrity and provides a modular strategy with the potential to integrate different 3'-end capture platforms. Performance validation demonstrated high concordance in global transcriptomic profiles and spatial gene expression patterns between nanoforest-derived replicas and conventional tissue sections, as well as faithful recapitulation of pathological features in a traumatic brain injury (TBI) model. Furthermore, longitudinal spatial transcriptomic profiling of cortical injury in the same mouse revealed temporally distinct injury responses, progressive activation of immune-associated gene programs, and spatially heterogeneous cell-type-specific expression changes. By enabling repeated molecular sampling and spatial transcriptomic analysis of living tissue, LIFE-seq provides a versatile framework for investigating tissue dynamics and pathological progression in vivo.

papers.title: Age-dependent phosphorylation of estrogen receptor beta (ERβ) regulates homodimer formation and impairs the repression of amyloid precursor protein (APP) promoter.
papers.abstract: Estrogen receptor beta (ER{beta}) is a ligand-activated nuclear steroid receptor that promotes neuroprotection through its transcriptional coordination of healthy cell gene programs. However, circulating estrogens are dramatically reduced post-menopause and the administration of hormone replacement therapy is only beneficial within a narrowly restricted timeframe after the menopause transition. The molecular underpinnings for this failure of ER{beta} to evoke protection in advanced age is unknown. Evidence suggests that age-related changes in protein-protein interactions could preclude ER{beta} genomic signaling. Protein-protein interactions can be regulated and modified through post-translational modifications (PTM)s of individual amino acid residues; the most well-studied PTM being phosphorylation. Our prior work showed that ER{beta} phosphorylation was age-dependent leading to the hypothesis that ER{beta} phosphorylation is required for ER{beta}-protein interactions, specifically ER{beta} homodimer formation. We used fluorescence lifetime measurements to quantify Forster resonance energy transfer (FRET) of ER{beta}-S176, S200, and Y488 phosphomutant protein interactions. Overall, our results demonstrate that phosphorylation of ER{beta}-S176, S200, and Y488 reduced ER{beta} homodimer formation, suggesting an age-dependent molecular mechanism that regulates ER{beta} genomic signaling. Moreover, phosphorylation at S200 and Y488 resulted in a loss of ER{beta}-mediated amyloid precursor protein (APP) promoter gene repression providing evidence that these age-dependent PTMs directly impact ER{beta}'s function as a transcription factor. Taken together, these data suggest that age-dependent changes in ER{beta} phosphorylation result in decreased ER{beta} genomic signaling, which could reduce the neuroprotective effects of estrogens following menopause.
